definition: Renovate means to restore a building or other large structure to a good state of repair through major work, making it look newer and better.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word renovate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know renovate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The Okafor sisters spent two summers working to renovate the old wooden sailboat, sanding the hull and replacing every rotted plank.
Redecorate is weaker than renovate; redecorating changes paint and curtains, while renovating repairs the structure itself.
Rebuild is stronger than renovate; a renovated structure keeps its original bones, but a rebuilt one is torn down and constructed all over again.

Remodel means to change the structure or style of a space — knock out a wall, move the kitchen, reshape the layout. Renovate means restoring a structure to good repair through major work: it fixes and freshens what is there. Remodeling changes the design; renovating brings the existing design back.

Refurbish means to brighten up and repair something so it looks and works like new — cleaning, repainting, replacing small parts. It is the lighter job. Renovate implies major structural work on a building or large structure: floors leveled, cabinets ripped out, rot replaced.

Modernize means to update something to current standards — new wiring, new fixtures, a contemporary look. It is about bringing things up to date. Renovate is about bringing them back to good condition, which can mean faithfully restoring an old look rather than updating anything.

The kitchen had fallen into disrepair, and the family repaired its structure and updated its look until it was in good condition again.
Restoring a space to a solid, newer, better state is exactly what renovate means.
The go-to verb for fixing up buildings and rooms: renovate a house, a kitchen, or a stadium.
It implies real repair work, so it is stronger than redecorate, which only changes surfaces like paint and furniture.
Remember that people and reputations are rehabilitated, not renovated.

The Palace Cinema had gone dark in 1998, and twenty years of leaks had done their work: buckled aisles, sagging balcony, plaster falling in sheets.
When the arts trust bought it, the newspapers assumed the block would become condos.
Instead the trust announced it would renovate -- a promise that meant jacks under the balcony, new steel in the roof, and every seat unbolted so the floor could be rebuilt.
Nothing about the design changed.
The gilded ceiling was repaired square by square until it matched the 1931 photographs.
On opening night the marquee lit up exactly as it had ninety years earlier, over a building finally sound enough to hold the crowd.
